prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff requester.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an agency withholding records under FOIA bears the burden of showing that a claimed exemption applies, through detailed and non-conclusory declarations.

Cite at least six decisions of the D.C. Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

**The Agency Bears the Burden of Proving, Through Detailed and Non-Conclusory Declarations, That Each Claimed Exemption Applies.**

FOIA places the burden squarely on the withholding agency. The district court must "determine the matter de novo," and "the burden is on the agency to sustain its action." 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B); *see U.S. Dep't of State v. Ray*, 502 U.S. 164, 173 (1991); *U.S. Dep't of Just. v. Tax Analysts*, 492 U.S. 136, 142 n.3 (1989). Plaintiff need not prove that withheld records are subject to release. The Agency must prove that they are not. *See Citizens for Resp. & Ethics in Wash. v. U.S. Dep't of Just.*, 746 F.3d 1082, 1088 (D.C. Cir. 2014); *Summers v. Dep't of Just.*, 140 F.3d 1077, 1080 (D.C. Cir. 1998). That burden carries particular force because FOIA's exemptions are narrowly construed. *Milner v. Dep't of the Navy*, 562 U.S. 562, 565 (2011); *Citizens for Resp. & Ethics*, 746 F.3d at 1088.

An agency may attempt to carry its burden by declaration, but only if the declaration does real work. Summary judgment is warranted on agency affidavits when they "describe the justifications for nondisclosure with reasonably specific detail, demonstrate that the information withheld logically falls within the claimed exemption, and are not controverted by either contrary evidence in the record nor by evidence of agency bad faith." *Larson v. Dep't of State*, 565 F.3d 857, 862 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (citation omitted); *see ACLU v. U.S. Dep't of Def.*, 628 F.3d 612, 619 (D.C. Cir. 2011). Each condition matters. A declaration that lacks specificity, fails to connect the withheld material to the exemption, or is contradicted by the record cannot support judgment for the Agency.

To be sure, an agency's justification is sufficient if it appears "logical" or "plausible." *Wolf v. CIA*, 473 F.3d 370, 374–75 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (citation omitted); *Larson*, 565 F.3d at 862. But plausibility is measured against facts the agency actually supplies. It does not permit a court to accept assertion in place of explanation. Affidavits will not suffice if they are "conclusory, merely reciting statutory standards, or if they are too vague or sweeping." *Quiñon v. FBI*, 86 F.3d 1222, 1227 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (citation omitted). This Court has accordingly refused to sustain withholdings where the agency's declaration failed to tie the particular material withheld to the governing exemption standard. *See Campbell v. U.S. Dep't of Just.*, 164 F.3d 20, 30–31 (D.C. Cir. 1998).

The agency must instead provide "a relatively detailed justification, specifically identifying the reasons why a particular exemption is relevant and correlating those claims with the particular part of a withheld document to which they apply." *Jud. Watch, Inc. v. FDA*, 449 F.3d 141, 146 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (citation omitted). Whether presented in a declaration, a *Vaughn* index, or both, the substance controls. The submission must identify what was withheld, state which exemption covers each withholding, and explain why. Without that information, the requester, who has not seen the records, cannot meaningfully contest the claim, and the court cannot perform de novo review.

The same burden extends to segregability. "Any reasonably segregable portion of a record shall be provided" after exempt portions are deleted. 5 U.S.C. § 552(b). District courts have an affirmative duty to consider segregability, even if the requester does not raise it. *Trans-Pac. Policing Agreement v. U.S. Customs Serv.*, 177 F.3d 1022, 1027–28 (D.C. Cir. 1999). Although agencies receive a presumption of compliance that a requester must rebut with some evidence, *Sussman v. U.S. Marshals Serv.*, 494 F.3d 1106, 1117 (D.C. Cir. 2007), a court may not approve withholding of entire documents without making specific findings on segregability. *Id.* at 1116. Moreover, for requests governed by the FOIA Improvement Act of 2016, establishing that an exemption applies may not end the inquiry: absent a legal prohibition on disclosure, the agency may withhold only if it reasonably foresees that disclosure would harm an interest the exemption protects, or if disclosure is prohibited by law. 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(i).

Unless the Agency's declarations meet these requirements for every withholding, it has not carried its burden, and summary judgment in its favor must be denied or, on appeal, reversed.
